title: Programming in Python
summary: Types, mutability, copies, identity, and the costs of list and dict operations, traced on short snippets that actually run.
intuition:
A Python value has a type, and the type decides whether an operation builds a new object or changes the old one. Integers, floats, strings, and tuples are immutable: an assignment such as `s + "!"` produces a new string. Lists, dicts, and sets are mutable: `append`, item assignment, and `add` change the object that existing names already point at. Two names can refer to one list. A slice is a new list.

Indexing starts at $0$. The last element is at index $-1$. `==` asks whether values are equal. `is` asks whether two names refer to the same object. Equal lists are not automatically the same object, and CPython interns small integers, so a test that used `is` on the number $3$ can fail on $3000$. A mutable default argument is evaluated once, when the function is defined, and then shared by later calls.

Loops are `for` over a sequence and `while` with an explicit index. A function returns a value; a recursive function needs a base case. The costs that are worth memorising are short. `append` and `pop()` at the end of a list are amortised $O(1)$. `insert(0, x)` and `pop(0)` shift every later element, so they are $O(n)$. Dict and set lookup are average $O(1)$ and worst-case $O(n)$.

$$\text{append is amortised }O(1),\qquad \text{insert}(0)\text{ is }O(n).$$

definitions.body: A mutable object can be changed without creating a new object. Lists, dicts, and sets are mutable. Integers, floats, booleans, strings, and tuples are immutable. Item assignment on a tuple raises `TypeError`.
An assignment binds a name to an object. After `b = a` with `a` a list, `a` and `b` are the same list. A later `b.append(...)` or `b[0] = ...` is visible through `a`.
The slice `a[:]` is a new list containing the same elements. Mutating the new list does not mutate `a`, and mutating `a` does not mutate the slice. A slice of a list of lists is a shallow copy.
`a == b` compares values. `a is b` compares object identity. Two separately built lists with the same items satisfy `==` and fail `is`. Do not use `is` to test numeric equality.
A default such as `acc=[]` is created once. Every call that omits the argument receives that same list. Values appended on one call are still there on the next call.

formulas.name: End of a list
formulas.note: Occasional resizing copies the whole list. Across a sequence of appends the average cost per append is constant.

formulas.name: Front of a list
formulas.note: Every element after the front moves one slot. A stack uses the end of the list. A queue does not use `pop(0)`.

formulas.name: Dict and set
formulas.note: Average lookup assumes hashing spreads the keys. A collision chain of length $n$ makes one lookup linear.

formulas.name: Summation by recursion
formulas.note: Then $s(n)=n(n+1)/2$. The base case is what stops the calls.

properties: Indexing starts at $0$. For a list of length $n$ the legal indexes run from $0$ through $n-1$, and index $-1$ is the last element.
`list.append` and `list.pop()` are amortised $O(1)$. `list.insert(0, x)` and `list.pop(0)` are $O(n)$ because they move the tail.
A dict lookup and a set membership test are average $O(1)$ and worst-case $O(n)$. Building `{1, 1, 2, 3}` keeps three elements, because a set stores each value once.
Slicing copies. After `c = a[:]` and a later mutation of `a` through another name, `c` still holds the old items. `a is b` can be true while `a == c` is false.
A recursive call without a base case does not return. `fact(0)` must return $1$ so that `fact(5)` can unwind as $5\cdot 4\cdot 3\cdot 2\cdot 1=120$.

examples.title: Alias, slice, and a shared default list
examples.prompt: The lesson snippet binds `b = a` and `c = a[:]` for `a = [10, 20, 30]`, then sets `b[0] = 99`. It also calls `collect(\"p\")` and `collect(\"q\")`, where `collect` appends to a default list and returns a copy of that list. Trace the first two printed lines.
steps: Before the assignment, `a` is `[10, 20, 30]`. The name `b` refers to that same list, so `a is b` is true. The slice `c = a[:]` copies the three integers into a new list.
The assignment `b[0] = 99` changes the shared list. Afterwards `a` is `[99, 20, 30]` and `a[0]` prints as $99$. The copy `c` is still `[10, 20, 30]`, so `c[0]` is $10$ and `a == c` is false.
`collect(\"p\")` appends to the default list, which was empty, and returns a new list equal to `['p']`. `collect(\"q\")` appends to that same default list, so the returned copy is `['p', 'q']`.
The first printed line is `(99, 10, True, False)`. The second is `(['p'], ['p', 'q'])`. The snippet asserts both tuples.
examples.answer: The printout begins with `(99, 10, True, False)` and then `(['p'], ['p', 'q'])`. The slice protected `c`. The default list remembered `p`.

examples.title: Recursion, a front insert, and a while loop
examples.prompt: In the same snippet, trace `fact(5)`, `insert(0, 9)` on `[1, 2, 3]`, and the while loop that sums `[4, 5, 6, 7]`.
steps: `row` starts as `[1, 2, 3]`. `insert(0, 9)` shifts the three existing elements one slot to the right and writes $9$ at index $0$. The list becomes `[9, 1, 2, 3]`. That shift is why `insert(0)` is $O(n)$.
The while loop starts at index $0$. It adds `data[0]+data[1]+data[2]+data[3]=4+5+6+7=22` and stops when the index equals the length $4$. A `for` loop over the same list adds the same $22$.
The snippet asserts `row == [9, 1, 2, 3]`, `fact(5) == 120`, and `total == 22`, and it prints those three results on the third line.
examples.answer: `fact(5)` is $120$, the list after the front insert is `[9, 1, 2, 3]`, and the loop total is $22$.

traps: Assuming `b = a` copies a list. It binds a second name. A slice `a[:]` or a call to `list(a)` is the copy.
Using `is` to compare numbers. `int(\"3000\") == int(\"3000\")` is true and `int(\"3000\") is int(\"3000\")` is false. Small integers are interned, so the same test on $3$ can pass by accident.
Expecting a fresh list from a mutable default. `def f(x, acc=[])` shares one list across calls, so the lengths returned by three calls are $1$, $2$, and $3$, not $1$, $1$, and $1$.
Treating `insert(0, x)` as an amortised constant, the way `append` is. The front insert moves every element and is $O(n)$. Index $0$ is the first element, not the second.
python:
def collect(x, bag=[]):
    bag.append(x)
    return list(bag)

a = [10, 20, 30]
b = a
c = a[:]
b[0] = 99
line1 = (a[0], c[0], a is b, a == c)
line2 = (collect("p"), collect("q"))
assert line1 == (99, 10, True, False)
assert line2 == (["p"], ["p", "q"])

row = [1, 2, 3]
row.insert(0, 9)
assert row == [9, 1, 2, 3]

def fact(n):
    return 1 if n == 0 else n * fact(n - 1)

data = [4, 5, 6, 7]
total = 0
i = 0
while i < len(data):
    total += data[i]
    i += 1
assert fact(5) == 120 and total == 22 and data[0] == 4 and data[-1] == 7
assert len({1, 1, 2, 3}) == 3
left, right = [1], [1]
assert left == right and not (left is right)
assert int("3000") == int("3000") and not (int("3000") is int("3000"))

def s(n):
    return 0 if n == 0 else n + s(n - 1)

assert s(10) == 55
print(line1)
print(line2)
print(row, fact(5), total, s(10))

questions.stem: After `a = [1, 2, 3]`, `b = a`, `c = a[:]`, and `b.append(4)`, what does `print(len(a), len(c), a is b)` show?
questions.solution:
The answer is **A**, `4 3 True`.

`b = a` binds both names to one list, so `a is b` stays true and `append` changes that list from length $3$ to length $4$. The slice `c = a[:]` was taken before the append, and slicing copies, so `c` still has length $3$. Option B would be right if the slice were another alias. Option D would be right if `b = a` had copied.

questions.stem: A function is defined by `def f(x, acc=[]):` then `acc.append(x)` and `return len(acc)`. What does `print(f(10), f(20), f(30))` show?
questions.solution:
The answer is **A**, `1 2 3`.

The default list is created once. The first call appends $10$ and returns length $1$. The second appends $20$ to that same list and returns length $2$. The third returns length $3$. A fresh list on every call would have printed `1 1 1`. The return value is the length, not the appended integer, so `10 20 30` is the contents rather than the printout.

questions.stem: Which of the following are true?
options: `==` compares values and `is` compares object identity.
Average-case lookup in a Python dict is $O(1)$.
questions.solution:
The correct options are **A and C**.

Equality is `==`. Identity is `is`. Two lists built separately can be equal and not identical. Dict lookup is average $O(1)$, with a linear worst case when every key collides.

`insert(0, x)` moves every current element, so it is $O(n)$, unlike `append`. A tuple is immutable: assigning to `point[0]` raises `TypeError`.

questions.stem: Start with `xs = [10, 20, 30, 40]`, set `ys = xs[1:3]`, then set `ys[0] = 0`. Which of the following are true?
questions.solution:
The correct options are **A, B, and D**.

The slice `xs[1:3]` copies the items at indexes $1$ and $2$, namely $20$ and $30$. Assigning `ys[0] = 0` changes that copy, so `ys` becomes `[0, 30]`. Slicing copied, so `xs` is untouched and is still `[10, 20, 30, 40]`.

Index $0$ is the first element, $10$, not $20$. Index $-1$ is the last element, $40$.

questions.stem: Define `s(0) = 0` and `s(n) = n + s(n - 1)` for `n > 0`. Enter the integer `s(10)`.
questions.solution:
The answer is **55**.

Unwinding the recurrence gives $s(10)=10+9+\cdots+1+s(0)$. The sum of the integers from $1$ through $10$ is $10\cdot 11/2=55$, and the base case adds $0$. The same value is $s(9)+10=45+10$.
